procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Patna
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 08.06.2022 of the High Court of Judicature at Patna in CWJC No. 1375 of 2021 (Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 1375 of 2021)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court passed a judgment and order on 08.06.2022 in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 1375 of 2021.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant was aggrieved by the High Court's order and filed a Criminal Appeal (No. 4324 of 2024) in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the High Court.

directions: The impugned judgment and order dated 8th June 2022 passed by the learned Single Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Patna in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 1375 of 2021 is quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the CrPC when the ingredients of the alleged offences were not prima facie made out.

facts: An FIR was registered alleging offences under various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), including 420, 406, and 409.
The accused (an appellant-bank) filed a petition in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) seeking to quash the FIR.
The High Court dismissed the petition, refusing to quash the FIR.
law: Under Section 482 of the CrPC, a High Court has the inherent power to quash an FIR.

When considering a petition to quash an FIR, the High Court must conduct a prima facie inquiry to determine if the allegations in the FIR, taken at face value, constitute the essential ingredients of the alleged offence.
Citing the precedent in *State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal*, an FIR can be quashed if the uncontroverted allegations within it do not disclose the commission of any cognizable offence.
The principle that this jurisdiction should be exercised "sparingly" does not absolve the court of its duty to assess the contents of the specific FIR before it.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to perform its duty under Section 482 CrPC.
The High Court recited the legal position that the power to quash should be used sparingly but did not actually conduct a prima facie evaluation of the FIR's contents.
The Supreme Court conducted this exercise itself and found a clear "disconnect" between the allegations in the FIR and the offences alleged.

For example, the Court noted that the necessary ingredients for an offence under Section 420 IPC, such as dishonest inducement and mens rea from the inception, were not made out in the FIR's allegations against the bank.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was clearly in error for refusing to quash the FIR. It failed in its duty to conduct a prima facie analysis, which would have revealed that the ingredients of the alleged offences were not established by the allegations in the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offences of criminal breach of trust under Sections 406 and 409 of the Indian Penal Code were prima facie established from the FIR.

facts: The First Information Report (FIR) filed in the case did not contain any allegation that property had been entrusted to the accused bank.
law: To establish the offence of criminal breach of trust under Sections 406 and 409 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), a key ingredient is the "entrustment" of property.
Following the entrustment, it must be shown that the person entrusted with the property dishonestly misappropriated it, converted it to their own use, or dishonestly used or disposed of it.
application: The Court examined the allegations in the FIR to see if they met the legal requirements for criminal breach of trust.
It found that the FIR completely lacked the foundational allegation of "entrustment" of property to the accused bank.
Because there was no allegation of entrustment, the question of whether the bank misappropriated or converted any property could not arise under these sections.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the ingredients for the offences of criminal breach of trust under Sections 406 and 409 of the IPC were not established, because the FIR failed to allege the essential element of entrustment of property with the accused bank.

issue.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offence of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code were prima facie established from the FIR.

facts: An FIR was registered against an appellant-bank, a 'juristic person', for several offences, including cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The bank filed a petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to quash the FIR, arguing that the allegations did not constitute the alleged offences.
The High Court dismissed the bank's petition.
The Supreme Court examined the FIR to determine if the necessary elements of the offence of cheating were present on the face of the record.
law: To establish an offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC, the FIR must disclose three essential ingredients:
1. That the accused induced someone from the inception.
2. That this inducement was fraudulent or dishonest.
3. That 'mens rea' (a guilty or dishonest intention) existed at the very time of the inducement.
application: The Court analyzed the contents of the FIR at face value.
It found that there was nothing in the FIR to show that the bank or its staff had dishonestly induced anyone to deliver any property.
Specifically, the Court determined that the crucial ingredient of 'mens rea' existing at the time of the alleged inducement was absent from the allegations in the FIR.
The Court also noted that since the bank is a 'juristic person', the question of it having 'mens rea' does not arise in the same way as it would for a natural person.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the essential ingredients required to constitute the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC were not available or established from the FIR. Therefore, a prima facie case for cheating was not made out.

issue.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offence under Section 462 of the Indian Penal Code were applicable, particularly concerning the element of entrustment of property.

facts: There was no allegation that any property had been entrusted to the appellant-bank.
law: The offence under Section 462 of the Indian Penal Code requires the element of entrustment of property.
application: The Court examined the facts of the case and found that there was no entrustment of any property with the appellant-bank.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the applicability of Section 462 of the IPC because the essential ingredient of entrustment of property with the appellant-bank was absent from the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the CrPC when the ingredients of the alleged offences were not prima facie made out.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court should have quashed the FIR because the allegations, even when taken at face value, did not disclose the essential ingredients of the offences mentioned. This argument is supported by their reliance on the principles laid down in cases like State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the court should not conduct an inquiry into the reliability or genuineness of the allegations in the FIR at the quashing stage, as that is a matter for investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offences of criminal breach of trust under Sections 406 and 409 of the Indian Penal Code were prima facie established from the FIR.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the essential element of 'entrustment' of property, which is necessary to constitute an offence of criminal breach of trust under Sections 406 and 409, was not made out from the FIR.
respondent_arguments: The respondent maintained that the allegations in the FIR were sufficient to prima facie establish the ingredients of criminal breach of trust, and the matter required further investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offence of cheating under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code were prima facie established from the FIR.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that a key ingredient of cheating, namely dishonest inducement from the very beginning, was absent. The text notes their specific contention that there was no allegation that 'the appellant-bank had induced anyone since inception'.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the allegations in the FIR, if taken as true, made out a case of cheating that warranted investigation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the ingredients of the offence under Section 462 of the Indian Penal Code were applicable, particularly concerning the element of entrustment of property.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that Section 462 was not applicable as the facts did not involve the entrustment of a closed receptacle for safe custody, a necessary element for this offence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that the actions described in the FIR fell within the scope of Section 462 and that the element of entrustment was present.

cases.case_name: Arnab Manoranjan Goswami v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
cases.principle: Cited for its observations on the principles relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

cases.case_name: State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others
cases.principle: Cited for the illustrative categories of cases where the High Court can exercise its extraordinary power under Article 226 or inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The extraordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure can be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
obiter: It may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that the continuation of the criminal proceedings against the appellant-bank would cause it undue hardship. This finding was based on the acceptance of the appellant's argument that the allegations in the FIR, even if taken at face value, did not prima facie constitute the essential ingredients of the alleged offences, warranting the quashing of the proceedings to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
legal_tests_applied: The principles for quashing an FIR under Section 482 of the CrPC as laid down in State of Haryana and others v. Bhajan Lal and others, which permit quashing where the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence.
policy_considerations: The Court intervened to prevent undue hardship and a miscarriage of justice that would result from the continuation of a criminal prosecution where the foundational ingredients of the alleged offences were not made out from the FIR.
